newsitem.title: USA: Dow, bonds fall but dollar up on strong data.
newsitem.headline: Dow, bonds fall but dollar up on strong data.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks fell on Wednesday as investors took profits one day after the market rallied on the Federal Reserve's decision to hold interest rates steady.
Bonds also slid, but the dollar rose as a sharp drop in the U.S. trade deficit signalled strong economic growth and lifted prospects that central bank would raise rates soon.
The Dow Jones industrial average closed down 12.77 points at 7,290.69 after soaring 75 points Tuesday.
But in the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,420 to 1,108 on heavy volume of 537 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Stocks surged initially, but then fell as much as 50 points under pressure from a weak bond market.

Bond prices slumped after the government said the nation's trade deficit plunged 19.3 percent to $8.51 billion in March, well below the $10.3 billion gap economist had forecast. Both imports and exports hit record highs.

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell nearly three-quarters of a point, which raised its yield to 6.96 percent from 6.90 percent at Tuesday's close. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

The trade numbers, which pointed to strong U.S. growth, particularly in the export sector, meant that the government might have to revise upward its estimate of 5.6 percent first quarter growth -- its fastest pace in more than nine years.
On Tuesday, the Fed kept interest rates unchanged in hopes that the economy would slow from its recent break-neck pace.

Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Nesbitt Burns, said the strength in exports was even more surprising because it came in the face of gains in the dollar, which had been strong in March before its recent fall.
Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer for First Albany, said bonds also were hurt by fears that the falling dollar might encourage foreign investors to switch out of U.S. Treasury bonds.
The dollar rose to 1.6943 German marks from 1.6770 at Tuesday's close and to 114.35 Japanese yen from 112.63.
Coffee prices surged again after coffee-exporting countries agreed to extend an agreement to limit their exports for another 12 months despite recent soaring world prices.
At the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee for July delivery closed 12.85 cents a pound higher 253.10 cents.

Copper prices also continued to rise. Copper for July delivery at COMEX in New York ended 0.35 cent a pound higher at 118.20 cents, touching a new life-of-contract high during the day and remaining at the highest levels seen in a year.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, prices for pork bellies closed with gains near the daily 3.00-cent a pound trading limit after a government report showed low stocks.
Pork bellies for July delivery closed 2.80 cents a pound higher at 93.35 cents.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index ended 34.5 points firmer at 4,642.0. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average finished down 490.85 points, or 2.41 percent, at 19,841.98.
